name: Marginal Man
label: Dischord
lede: Two guitars when DC hardcore had one, a senator's son on lead, a sociology-class band name, and a farewell that sold out the same room where it all started.

eras.title: Outside looking in
eras.text: Artificial Peace had just folded, and three of its members wanted something bigger and more tuneful. They added Kenny Inouye, a kid who was at every one of their shows, on second guitar, and walked onstage at the 9:30 Club as one of DC's first twin-guitar hardcore bands.

years.h: Marginal Man forms from three ex-members of Artificial Peace
years.p: Singer [[Steve Polcari|33611a9d-0a07-418b-ac27-b51a58f93561]], guitarist [[Pete Murray|6ab4a566-a279-441a-af5f-4d47459e1c18]] and drummer [[Mike Manos|2da8a8ac-dab6-4b39-9ca6-ce91fee93fcf]] add [[Kenny Inouye|a2ae807d-953b-496b-ac75-62d55c5f0afc]] on second guitar and [[Andre Lee|b9484df3-7dce-4c9b-be55-072f26ca9498]] on bass. Inouye says he got on their radar by going to all their shows.

years.h: Kenny Inouye names the band Marginal Man
years.p: Kenny Inouye says the name Marginal Man was his idea, lifted from a sociology class: someone partly assimilated into two or more cultures but fully into none.
years.xp: Steve Polcari has explained it the same way from the scene side: having friends in two or more groups without belonging to any one of them. For a band of Bethesda and DC kids caught between hardcore's first wave and whatever came next, it fit.

years.h: Marginal Man debut at the 9:30 Club's "555" show
years.p: Dischord dates Marginal Man's debut for DC crowds to the "555" concert at the 9:30 Club. Kenny Inouye remembers their first real show as two sold-out sets opening for [[Minor Threat|09037f07-42bc-46ac-a1ee-37f834451fee]].
years.xp:
Wikipedia lists an earlier warm-up: a basement show on November 19, 1982, with [[Scream|b9f52132-28af-4cea-9558-165cd125f9b7]], Insurrection, Double-O and [[United Mutation|40d5b767-7978-4956-8245-586c1dd0b01d]]. The 9:30 Club was the real introduction, per Dischord.

Two guitars set them apart. Most DC hardcore bands of 1981 and 1982 ran on one, and Marginal Man's layered sound pointed toward the more melodic records the city would make a few years later.

eras.title: One Dischord record, then the open road
eras.text: Identity was Marginal Man's one Dischord record and their calling card. When a second Dischord release didn't come together, they took Double Image to Gasatanka/Enigma and spent the mid-80s as one of the early DC bands to tour the country hard.

years.p: Marginal Man's only Dischord record, a 12" EP cut at Inner Ear. The cover art was by Manolo Lagdameo, the band's roadie.

q: We didn't get a no, but we also didn't get a yes.
years.h: Marginal Man take Double Image to Gasatanka/Enigma
years.p: Marginal Man's follow-up to Identity doesn't come out on Dischord. The band signs with Gasatanka/Enigma for Double Image.
years.xp:
Kenny Inouye has told it without bitterness: Dischord was in a shaky financial spot, and the band wanted the record out on time, so they looked elsewhere.

[[Brian Baker|1fd36abf-e43c-4b01-820b-d7280cc27ea5]] of Minor Threat helped shape Double Image, mostly by telling them what wasn't working. Etched in the inner groove: "70% of 0 is Pizza", a souvenir of a Denver show where the promoter paid them in pizza instead of door money.

years.p: Marginal Man's first full-length, on Gasatanka/Enigma. It returned on CD in 2000 through In Your Eye, distributed by Dischord.

years.h: Marginal Man on the Alive & Kicking compilation
years.p: Marginal Man joins Alive & Kicking, the WGNS compilation of the new DC wave.

Early tours ran DIY with roadie Manolo Lagdameo along. Marginal Man shared bills with the Circle Jerks, TSOL, [[Necros|a8971728-0985-4b30-a209-142784e7c3b8]] and Corrosion of Conformity, and Kenny Inouye credits Necros and COC with looking out for younger bands.

years.h: Full set at GWU's Marvin Center, 1985
yt: Full set at GWU's Marvin Center, 1985

eras.title: Going out on a high note
eras.text: By the late 80s Marginal Man's members were writing in different directions, and their self-titled final LP showed it. Rather than drift into being a legacy act, they booked two farewell shows at the 9:30 Club.

years.h: Marginal Man, the final LP, on Giant Records
years.p: A transitional record, with each writer pulling his own way. Kenny Inouye still counts some of his favorite songs on it.

years.h: Marginal Man's farewell: two sold-out shows at the 9:30
years.p: Marginal Man headline the 9:30 Club, where they debuted, with [[Shudder to Think|5a6e19e0-3ff0-4b3d-869e-3c539d6d8707]] opening both sets. Kenny Inouye says the choice was fade away or go out on a high note.

eras.title: Reunions and a booking desk
eras.text: Marginal Man kept coming back for single nights, and Kenny Inouye ended up booking the 9:30 Club, where the band had started. Dischord kept Identity in print on CD.

years.h: Marginal Man on State of the Union
years.p: A Marginal Man track on Dischord's 1989 compilation, Dischord No. 32.
Marginal Man play the first of several one-night reunions after the 1988 farewell.
Marginal Man play another one-night reunion show at year's end.
Dischord reissues Marginal Man's 1984 EP Identity on CD.

eras.title: One more at the Black Cat
eras.text: Twenty-three years after the farewell, the five members of Marginal Man played again, this time at the Black Cat, the club run by fellow DC veteran Dante Ferrando.

years.h: Marginal Man reunite at the Black Cat
years.p: The Washington Post previewed the Black Cat reunion as tracks from a formative period. Kenny Inouye had by then booked the 9:30 Club himself; he now works at the University of Hawaiʻi–West Oʻahu.
years.xp: Kenny Inouye's father was Senator Daniel Inouye, who came to several of Marginal Man's early shows.
